scenes.title: Seventeen thousand numbers
scenes.text: Seventeen thousand numbers. Which game did they learn? No labels. No code. Just the weights of a small neural network. An AI read them, and answered: Breakout.

scenes.title: Written by descent
scenes.text: Normally, no one reads weights like these, and no one writes them by hand. An optimizer does, nudging every number slightly downhill on a loss, millions of times over.

scenes.title: Ask in plain English
scenes.text: In November twenty twenty-six, four researchers at M I T see-sail tried something else. They handed raw weights to a frontier model, OpenAI's G P T six Astra, and asked in plain English. No training loop. No gradients. They call it weight-space programming.

scenes.title: Read: which game
scenes.text: First, reading. Four networks, identical in shape, each trained on a different grid game. Astra saw only the weights, with no list of games to choose from, and named all four. One clue: in Breakout, the player's first-layer weights pile up along the bottom row. A paddle.

scenes.title: Read: circuits
scenes.text: Then something harder. Three tiny language models, with their input and output layers cut away, so nothing says which letter is which. Without running them, just by multiplying weight matrices, Astra found every copying head, the circuit that repeats earlier text. Code repeats names, so many copying heads pointed to Python.

scenes.title: Fix: the car
scenes.text: Next, fixing. A trained car keeps stalling on a ramp. It never learned to back up for a run-up. In a single reply, Astra wired a small extra path through a few units per layer: reverse first, then hand back control. Three and a half percent of the weights changed, and the car succeeded in all one thousand and twenty-four episodes.

scenes.title: Write: from zero
scenes.text: Then, writing from nothing. Every weight starts at zero. Given the rules and source code of three miniature Atari games, Astra writes the weights as text. In Breakout, layer one works out where the ball will land. Layer two moves the paddle there. Scored without a single practice game, it beat P P O trained for a hundred million steps, in all three.

scenes.title: Write: Go
scenes.text: With one and a half million weights, too many to read at once, Astra gets a Python sandbox. It builds a Go player layer by layer: stones, liberties, groups in danger, a score for every move. Allowed fifty trial runs, it beat an equal-sized P P O network trained on twenty million games.

scenes.title: Improve: the loop
scenes.text: Now a real language model: Kwen three point five, with eight hundred million weights. It tends to get stuck thinking in loops. Eighty-five of its first ninety-six practice answers ran out of tokens. Astra traced the looping to a single direction, written by the M L P blocks of layers fifteen and nineteen.

scenes.title: Improve: the edit
scenes.text: In sixty-four columns of each, it subtracted that direction. A hundred and thirty-one thousand weights. Point zero one six percent of the model, and no gradients. On Math five hundred, accuracy rose from seven point nine to forty-eight point one percent, and instruction following tripled. In Astra's own check, a random direction of the same size barely helped.

scenes.title: Limits
scenes.text: The limits are real. From weights alone, Astra could not tell which of two models had been trained to simply agree with the user. It needed to see where their attention looked. And on Gemma, a model that rarely loops, its edits did not help. Removing an obstacle can reveal an ability. It could not add one the model lacked.

scenes.title: Read like a program
scenes.text: This is an early blog post with complete logs, not yet peer-reviewed, and the models are small. But for decades, weights were written by simple update rules. Here, a model reasoned about them, the way a programmer reads code. Seventeen thousand numbers, read like a program.
